prompt: What travels down a PowerShell pipeline between two commands?
hint: It is the one idea the whole language is built on.

choices.text: Lines of text, as in bash
choices.why: That is the Unix pipeline, and choosing otherwise is what makes PowerShell different.

choices.text: A rendered table, ready to print
choices.why: The table is drawn at the very end, by a formatter.

choices.text: Objects with named properties
choices.why: Yes, and the next command receives them rather than a rendering of them.

choices.text: A file handle the next command reads
choices.why: Nothing is written to a file or a buffer between stages.

prompt: You have an object and no idea what you can ask it. Which command answers that?
hint: It is the first one to learn.

choices.text: Get-Help
choices.why: It documents a command, not an object that came out of one.

choices.text: Get-Member
choices.why: Right. It prints the type and every property and method on it.

choices.text: Get-Command
choices.why: That finds commands by name, verb or noun.

choices.text: Format-List
choices.why: That shows the values it chooses to show, not what else is there.

prompt: `ls -l f | awk '{print $5}'` and `(Get-ChildItem f).Length` both give a file's size. Which problem does only the first one have?
hint: Lesson 8 measured this on a log where every line looked the same shape.

choices.text: It struggles with files over two gigabytes
choices.why: Both read the same number from the same place.

choices.text: It needs the file to exist first
choices.why: So does the other one, and it says so if it does not.

choices.text: It rounds the answer to the nearest kilobyte
choices.why: Neither rounds; `-l` prints exact bytes.

choices.text: It counts columns in a rendering
choices.why: Correct. A name with a space in it shifts every column after it.

prompt: PowerShell starts in about 0.4 seconds against bash's 0.003. When does that actually matter?
hint: Think about who or what is starting the shell, and how often.

choices.text: When a scheduler runs it every minute
choices.why: Yes — a hundred and thirty times the startup cost, repeated all day.

choices.text: When the script has a large file to process
choices.why: Startup is paid once whatever the file size is.

choices.text: When you are typing at a prompt
choices.why: Four tenths of a second is below what a person notices while typing.

choices.text: When the script is long
choices.why: The length of the file changes parsing time, not runtime startup.

prompt: Every PowerShell command is named `Verb-Noun`. What does the convention buy you?
hint: Think about a command whose name you have never seen.

choices.text: Faster execution, because the name is parsed once
choices.why: Names are not a performance question.

choices.text: You look one up by what it works on
choices.why: Correct — `Get-Command -Noun Service` lists everything that works on services.

choices.text: Two commands are prevented from sharing a name
choices.why: Modules can and do collide; the convention does not prevent it.

choices.text: The shell can tell a cmdlet apart from a native program
choices.why: That distinction comes from where the command is, not what it is called.

prompt: On PowerShell for Linux, `Get-Alias ls` reports that no such alias exists. On Windows it points at `Get-ChildItem`. Why the difference?
hint: What else is called `ls` on a Linux machine?

choices.text: Aliases are user settings and were not configured here
choices.why: They are created by PowerShell itself at startup.

choices.text: The Linux build ships fewer commands overall
choices.why: It ships fewer modules, but this is not about a missing cmdlet.

choices.text: A real `ls` program exists here and would be shadowed
choices.why: Right. PowerShell drops the alias so the native tool stays reachable.

choices.text: `Get-ChildItem` behaves differently on Linux
choices.why: It is the same cmdlet; only the alias differs.

prompt: Why should a script spell out `-Recurse` rather than the `-Rec` that works at a prompt?
hint: Think about a future version of the cmdlet.

choices.text: Abbreviations are slower to resolve
choices.why: The resolution cost is not measurable.

choices.text: Abbreviations work interactively and nowhere else
choices.why: They work everywhere; that is the problem.

choices.text: The shell warns about them in a file
choices.why: Nothing warns, which is why this is worth saying.

choices.text: A new parameter could make it ambiguous
choices.why: Correct. Your script breaks on an upgrade you did not make.

prompt: Match each discovery command to what it tells you.
hint: One of them is about an object rather than a command.

pairs.right: the approved word list every cmdlet name starts from
everything that acts on one kind of thing
how whoever wrote it expected it to be used

prompt: `Import-Csv sales.csv | Get-Member` shows `revenue` as `string revenue=8721`. What does that tell you?
hint: Look at the word before the property name.

choices.text: Import-Csv does not guess types
choices.why: Correct — every column comes back as text, whatever it looks like.

choices.text: The file has a formatting error in that column
choices.why: The file is fine; this is what the cmdlet always does.

choices.text: Get-Member displays each value as a string
choices.why: It prints the declared type, and other cmdlets show integers here.

choices.text: The column was quoted in the CSV
choices.why: Quoting in the file changes nothing about the resulting type.

prompt: `1..1000000 | ForEach-Object { $_ } | Select-Object -First 3` returns at once. What happened to the other 999,997?
hint: A PowerShell pipeline passes one object all the way down before starting the next.

choices.text: They were produced and discarded
choices.why: Producing a million objects would not have been instant.

choices.text: They were buffered and freed later
choices.why: Nothing was buffered; there was nothing to buffer.

choices.text: They were never produced
choices.why: Right. Select-Object had what it asked for and stopped the pipeline.

choices.text: They went to a background thread
choices.why: PowerShell ran the whole pipeline in one thread here.

prompt: What is the difference between `Select-Object Name` and `Select-Object -ExpandProperty Name`?
hint: One gives you a container, the other gives you what is in it.

choices.text: The second is faster on large collections
choices.why: Speed is not the distinction; what comes out is.

choices.text: The first gives containers, the second gives contents
choices.why: Correct, and it is why something downstream sometimes cannot find what you handed it.

choices.text: The first keeps the original type, the second converts to string
choices.why: The first produces a new PSCustomObject; the original type is gone either way.

choices.text: The second also removes duplicates
choices.why: Neither one de-duplicates; `Sort-Object -Unique` does.

prompt: Name the variable that holds the object currently going past inside a `ForEach-Object` block: `1..3 | ForEach-Object { ____ * 2 }`
hint: Two characters.

prompt: The same file and threshold give 16 rows with `$_.revenue -gt 30000` and 7 with `[int]$_.revenue -gt 30000`. What produced the 16?
hint: What type is the left-hand side, and what does PowerShell do to the right?

choices.text: Rows where revenue was blank counted as zero
choices.why: A blank would compare as an empty string, and would not be greater.

choices.text: The unquoted form matched on a substring
choices.why: `-gt` never does substring matching.

choices.text: Nine rows were duplicated in the file
choices.why: The file has 32 rows and no duplicates.

choices.text: An alphabetical comparison of two strings
choices.why: Correct. The right side is converted to the left's type, so 30000 became a string.

prompt: `"ANA" -eq "ana"` returns True. How do you ask the case-sensitive question?
hint: One letter, on the front of the operator.

choices.text: `-ceq`
choices.why: Right. `-c` in front makes any comparison operator case-sensitive.

choices.text: `-eq -CaseSensitive`
choices.why: Operators do not take parameters; that is cmdlet syntax.

choices.text: `-seq`
choices.why: There is no such operator.

choices.text: `-eq` with both sides cast to `[string]`
choices.why: They are already strings; the cast changes nothing.

prompt: `Get-ChildItem -Filter '*.log'` and `Get-ChildItem | Where-Object Name -like '*.log'` give the same answer. Why prefer the first?
hint: Which one builds an object for every file in the directory?

choices.text: `-Filter` understands regular expressions
choices.why: It takes a wildcard, and a narrower one than `-like`.

choices.text: `Where-Object` is unable to see hidden files
choices.why: Neither does by default; `-Force` is what changes that.

choices.text: The provider filters first
choices.why: Correct, and on a directory server or across a network that is the whole difference.

choices.text: `-Filter` is case-sensitive and safer
choices.why: Both are case-insensitive here.

prompt: `"web01" -contains $allowed` returns False even though `web01` is in `$allowed`. What went wrong?
hint: Which side of `-contains` is the collection?

choices.text: `-contains` compares case-sensitively
choices.why: It does not; `-ccontains` is the case-sensitive one.

choices.text: The collection has to be on the left
choices.why: Correct. Written that way it asks whether one string contains a two-element array.

choices.text: `$allowed` needs to be cast to an array first
choices.why: It already is an array; the operands are the wrong way round.

choices.text: `-contains` works on strings, not arrays
choices.why: It is specifically the collection membership operator.

prompt: Lesson 8 warned that `uniq -c` on unsorted input gives a wrong answer. Why does `Group-Object` not have that problem?
hint: What does `uniq` actually collapse?

choices.text: It sorts its input first, internally
choices.why: It does not sort, and its output is in first-seen order.

choices.text: It refuses unsorted input with an error
choices.why: It accepts anything and reports correctly.

choices.text: It accepts objects, which arrive already ordered
choices.why: Objects arrive in whatever order the previous command emitted them.

choices.text: It groups by value rather than by adjacency
choices.why: Correct — `uniq` collapses runs, and `Group-Object` keeps a bucket per distinct value.

prompt: `Sort-Object revenue -Descending` puts 8721 at the top of a file whose largest revenue is 43731. Why?
hint: The property came out of Import-Csv.

choices.text: It sorted the values as text
choices.why: Right — `8` beats `4`, and the answer is plausible and wrong.

choices.text: `-Descending` reverses twice on numeric data
choices.why: It reverses once, whatever the type.

choices.text: The file is not sorted, so the result is undefined
choices.why: `Sort-Object` does not care what order its input arrives in.

choices.text: Just the first page of results was sorted
choices.why: It is a blocking stage: it sees everything before emitting anything.

prompt: Why does `Select-Object -First 3` belong after `Sort-Object` rather than before it?
hint: What does each of them need in order to do its job?

choices.text: `Select-Object` is unable to end a pipeline
choices.why: It can, and often is.

choices.text: `Sort-Object` refuses input shorter than its buffer
choices.why: It sorts whatever it is given, including three objects.

choices.text: Three arbitrary objects are not the top three
choices.why: Correct. `Sort-Object` has to see everything, so it goes first and the take goes after.

choices.text: `-First` counts from the end when it follows a sort
choices.why: It counts from the start wherever it is.

prompt: One cmdlet replaces `sort | uniq -c` from lesson 8. Name it: `Import-Csv f | ____ region`
hint: Two words with a hyphen.

prompt: `Import-Csv f | Format-Table | Where-Object region -eq north | Measure-Object` reports a count of zero, and eight rows match. What did Where-Object receive?
hint: Ask Get-Member what came out of the formatter.

choices.text: The eight rows, with their properties renamed
choices.why: Nothing was renamed; the rows are not there at all.

choices.text: Formatting instructions, not sales records
choices.why: Correct. `FormatStartData` and friends have no `region` on them, so nothing matched.

choices.text: Not a thing — Format-Table consumes its input
choices.why: Objects did come out — just a different kind.

choices.text: A single string containing the whole table
choices.why: It is a stream of objects, not one string.

prompt: A function returns a value with `Write-Host` and the caller gets nothing. Why?
hint: Which of the two writing cmdlets puts an object in the pipeline?

choices.text: Write-Host needs a `-PassThru` switch
choices.why: There is no such switch on it.

choices.text: The value was converted to a string and lost
choices.why: No conversion happened; nothing was emitted at all.

choices.text: Write-Host works inside a script but not a function
choices.why: It works in both, and does the same thing in both.

choices.text: It writes to the host, bypassing the pipeline
choices.why: Correct. It cannot be captured or redirected, which is exactly its purpose.

prompt: You want a pipeline's results in a file for another program to read. Which one?
hint: Formatting is for people reading a screen.

choices.text: ConvertTo-Json
choices.why: Yes — data the other side can parse, and `ConvertFrom-Json` reads it back.

choices.text: Format-Table > out.txt
choices.why: That writes the table a human would have read, headers and all.

choices.text: Out-Host -Paging > out.txt
choices.why: That is a pager, for a person, and it writes nothing useful.

choices.text: Format-List | Out-File
choices.why: Same problem: a rendering, with the labels in it.

prompt: `@{a=@{b=@{c=@{d=1}}}} | ConvertTo-Json` produces `"c": "System.Collections.Hashtable"`. What is the fix?
hint: The cmdlet has a parameter about how far down it goes.

choices.text: Convert each level separately and join them
choices.why: That is a great deal of work to replace one parameter.

choices.text: Use `[ordered]` hashtables so the order is stable
choices.why: Ordering is a different concern and does not affect depth.

choices.text: Pass `-Depth 10`
choices.why: Right. The default is 2 and anything deeper becomes the type name.

choices.text: Pipe through `ConvertFrom-Json` first
choices.why: That parses JSON; there is no JSON yet.

prompt: `"42" + 1` gives 421 and `42 + "1"` gives 43. What rule explains both?
hint: Something is converted. The question is which side.

choices.text: Numbers are converted to strings when mixed
choices.why: That would make the second answer 421 as well.

choices.text: The right operand is converted to the left's type
choices.why: Correct, and it is the same rule behind the comparison trap in filtering.

choices.text: Quoted values are treated as text throughout
choices.why: The second line has a quoted value and still added.

choices.text: The result takes the type of whichever side is longer
choices.why: Length is not consulted.

prompt: `"$f.Name"` prints the whole path followed by `.Name`. What did you want?
hint: The variable expanded on its own and stopped there.

choices.why: Braces delimit a variable name, and a dot is not part of one.

choices.text: `"$f->Name"`
choices.why: That arrow is not PowerShell syntax.

choices.text: `'$($f.Name)'`, with single quotes
choices.why: Single quotes expand nothing at all.
Right. `$( )` runs an expression inside a double-quoted string.

prompt: In a PowerShell double-quoted string, what is the escape character?
hint: It is not the one you are used to.

choices.text: A backtick
choices.why: Yes — `` `n `` is a newline, and backslash is an ordinary character.

choices.text: A backslash
choices.why: That is an ordinary character here, which is why Windows paths are easy to write.

choices.text: A caret
choices.why: That is `cmd.exe`'s escape character, not PowerShell's.

choices.text: A percent sign
choices.why: That is an alias for `ForEach-Object`.

prompt: `"hello".Trim` prints a list of signatures instead of trimming. What is missing?
hint: One is a method and one is a property.

choices.text: A cast to `[string]` first
choices.why: It is already a string; that is how it has a Trim at all.

choices.text: An argument saying what to trim
choices.why: Trim works with no argument, which is one of the signatures printed.

choices.text: The parentheses
choices.why: Right. A method without them is the method itself, and PowerShell prints its overloads.

choices.text: A `$` before the string literal
choices.why: Literals do not take a `$`; that is for variables.

prompt: A loop builds a result with `$results += $item` and gets slow at ten thousand items. Why?
hint: PowerShell arrays are a fixed size.

choices.text: Each `+=` copies the array into a new one
choices.why: Correct — and the cost grows with every iteration.

choices.text: `+=` on an array is a string concatenation
choices.why: It appends an element; the array stays an array.

choices.text: The garbage collector runs after each append
choices.why: Collection is not triggered per statement.

choices.text: Arrays are stored on disk above a certain size
choices.why: Nothing about arrays touches the disk.

prompt: Why does `$h.Keys` on `@{ name = 'web01'; port = 8080 }` print `port` first?
hint: Look at what a plain `@{ }` promises about order.

choices.text: The keys are sorted alphabetically
choices.why: `name` would come first if they were.

choices.text: A hashtable does not preserve insertion order
choices.why: Correct — same as bash's associative arrays, and `[ordered]@{ }` is the fix.

choices.text: The shorter key is emitted first
choices.why: Length plays no part in it.

choices.text: `Keys` returns them in reverse order of writing
choices.why: It is not reversed either; there is no order to reverse.

prompt: Why write `@(Get-ChildItem *.log).Count` rather than `(Get-ChildItem *.log).Count`?
hint: Think about a match of exactly one file, on an older version.

choices.text: `@( )` sorts the results first
choices.why: It does not sort; it only guarantees an array.

choices.text: One result comes back without that property
choices.why: Correct, and on Windows PowerShell 5.1 that is exactly what happens.

choices.text: `@( )` removes duplicate filenames
choices.why: Nothing is de-duplicated.

choices.text: Without it the wildcard stays unexpanded, as text
choices.why: The glob is expanded by the cmdlet either way.

prompt: Match each operator or spelling to what it produces.
hint: Two of them turn one thing into the other.

pairs.right: a hashtable that keeps its key order

right_distractors: a sorted copy of a collection

prompt: A setting read from a file holds the text `false`, and `if ($setting) { }` runs the block. Why?
hint: What makes a string truthy?

choices.text: The file had trailing whitespace
choices.why: Whitespace is not what decided this.

choices.text: `if` accepts booleans alone and coerced it wrongly
choices.why: It accepts any expression and evaluates its truthiness.

choices.text: PowerShell reads `false` as the keyword `$false`
choices.why: It does not; `$false` and the string `false` are different things.

choices.text: A non-empty string is true, whatever it says
choices.why: Correct — `[bool]"false"` is True, and that is the bug.

prompt: `switch (3) { 1 { "one" } 3 { "three" } 3 { "three again" } }` prints two lines. How does this differ from bash's `case`?
hint: Where does each of them stop?

choices.text: Every matching branch runs, not just the first
choices.why: Correct, and `break` inside a branch is how you stop it.

choices.text: The branches are evaluated in reverse order
choices.why: They run top to bottom, as written.

choices.text: `switch` compares as strings and matched twice
choices.why: It matched twice because both patterns are 3, not because of a type.

choices.text: `default` ran as well as the match
choices.why: There is no `default` in that line.

prompt: What is `Set-StrictMode -Version Latest` the PowerShell equivalent of?
hint: It is about names that were never assigned.

choices.text: `set -e`
choices.why: That is `$ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'`.

choices.text: `set -o pipefail`
choices.why: PowerShell pipelines do not have per-stage exit statuses to combine.

choices.text: `set -u`
choices.why: Right. An uninitialised variable becomes an error instead of `$null`.

choices.text: `shopt -s nullglob`
choices.why: That is about globs matching nothing, which PowerShell handles differently.

prompt: When should you use `ForEach-Object` rather than the `foreach` keyword?
hint: One of them needs the whole collection in memory first.

choices.text: When the collection is small and already in a variable
choices.why: That is the case where `foreach` wins on speed.

choices.text: When the objects are still arriving slowly
choices.why: Correct — it streams, so work starts before the last object exists.

choices.text: When you need `break` to leave the loop
choices.why: `break` is the one thing that works better in `foreach`.

choices.text: When the block assigns to a variable outside it
choices.why: Both can do that; scope is not the distinction.

prompt: `Get-Doubled -Number "twelve"` fails before the function body runs. What made that happen?
hint: Look at what is in front of the parameter name.

choices.text: A `Test-Path` check on the function's first line
choices.why: The function body never ran at all.

choices.text: `[CmdletBinding()]` on the function
choices.why: That adds common parameters; it does not type anything.

choices.text: `[int]` on the parameter in the `param` block
choices.why: Correct. PowerShell converts and rejects before the body is entered.

choices.text: `Set-StrictMode` being on
choices.why: Strict mode is about unset variables, not argument types.

prompt: A function takes pipeline input, two objects are piped in, and it reports only the last. What is missing?
hint: There are three blocks, and one of them runs per object.

choices.text: A `process { }` block
choices.why: Correct. Without it the body is one big `end`, run once after everything arrived.

choices.text: A `begin { }` block
choices.why: That runs once before, which is not where the per-object work goes.

choices.text: `[Parameter(ValueFromPipeline)]`
choices.why: It has that already, which is how the last object got in.

choices.text: A `foreach` inside the body
choices.why: The body does not receive a collection; it receives one object.

prompt: In bash a function's variables are global unless you say `local`. In PowerShell?
hint: The defaults are the other way round.

choices.text: The same: global unless declared otherwise
choices.why: That is bash's default, and it is why section 150 had to insist on `local`.

choices.text: Confined to the function, unless you say otherwise
choices.why: Correct, and needing one of those is usually a sign the function should return a value.

choices.text: Local, and the caller's variables are unreachable from it
choices.why: There is a way; it is just explicit.

choices.text: Global, but restored when the function returns
choices.why: Nothing restores them, in either language.

prompt: Complete the attribute that makes PowerShell reject a bad value before your code runs: `[____('Table','Json','Csv')] [string]$As`
hint: Two words run together, starting with Validate.

prompt: `Get-ChildItem Env:` lists environment variables and `Get-ChildItem C:\` lists files. What makes that possible?
hint: Both are trees, and something makes trees look alike.

choices.text: Env: is a folder the shell creates at startup
choices.why: Nothing is created on disk; there is no folder anywhere.

choices.text: Get-ChildItem has a special case for each one
choices.why: The cmdlet has no idea what it is listing.

choices.text: A provider presents each as a drive
choices.why: Correct — the same four cmdlets then work on all of them.

choices.text: The environment is stored in a file underneath
choices.why: It lives in the process, and is never written out.

prompt: `Get-ChildItem > out.txt` writes a table with headers, and `Get-ChildItem | Set-Content out.txt` writes bare paths. Why the difference?
hint: One of them goes through the formatter.

choices.text: One renders a picture, the other writes values
choices.why: Correct, and it is section 164's rule showing up where you did not expect it.

choices.text: Set-Content adds a header when it is told to
choices.why: It never adds one; the header came from the other side.

choices.text: `>` uses the console width and Set-Content does not
choices.why: Width affects the layout, not whether there is a table.

choices.text: They write the file in different encodings entirely
choices.why: Encoding differs in some versions and is not what produced the headers.

prompt: What does `Select-String` give you that `grep -n` does not?
hint: Think about what you do with the line number afterwards.

choices.text: Case-insensitive matching by default
choices.why: `grep -i` does that, and `Select-String` being insensitive by default is a separate surprise.

choices.text: Recursive search down through directories
choices.why: `grep -r` does that too.

choices.text: Regular expressions rather than fixed strings
choices.why: `grep` has taken regular expressions since 1973.

choices.text: Objects, with a usable line number on them
choices.why: Correct — no second step to cut the number back out of the text.

prompt: Name the cmdlet that answers `test -e`: `if (____ /etc/hosts) { "it is there" }`
hint: Two words with a hyphen.

prompt: A `try` block around `Get-Content /etc/nosuchfile` never enters its `catch`, and the error is printed anyway. What is missing?
hint: There are two classes of error and `catch` only sees one.

choices.text: A `finally` block written after the catch
choices.why: `finally` runs afterwards; it does not make anything catchable.

choices.text: `-ErrorAction Stop` on the cmdlet
choices.why: Correct — a non-terminating error is reported and stepped over, catch or no catch.

choices.text: `Set-StrictMode -Version Latest`
choices.why: That is about unset variables, not about errors.

choices.text: A `throw` inside the try block
choices.why: Adding one would be caught, and would not catch the original.

prompt: After a cmdlet fails, `$LASTEXITCODE` still holds 2 from an `ls` two lines earlier. What does that tell you?
hint: One of the two status variables is only touched by one kind of command.

choices.text: The cmdlet failed with the same code by coincidence
choices.why: It set no code at all, which is the point.

choices.text: `$LASTEXITCODE` accumulates the worst status seen
choices.why: It holds the most recent one, not a running maximum.

choices.text: Cmdlets do not set `$LASTEXITCODE`
choices.why: Correct — it is stale until the next native program, so reading it after a cmdlet is reading history.

choices.text: The cmdlet ran a native program internally
choices.why: `Get-Content` starts no process.

prompt: Which pair is the PowerShell equivalent of `set -euo pipefail` at the top of a script?
hint: One line for unset names, one for failures.

choices.text: `Set-StrictMode` and `$ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'`
choices.why: Yes, and neither notices a native program that returned 1.

choices.text: `$ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'` and `trap { }`
choices.why: A `trap` handles errors; it does not catch unset variables.

choices.text: `Set-StrictMode -Version Latest` and `$ErrorView = 'DetailedView'`
choices.why: `$ErrorView` changes how an error is printed.

choices.text: `-ErrorAction Stop` and `-WarningAction Stop`
choices.why: Those are per-command parameters, not script-wide settings.

prompt: A script runs `git clone $url` and carries on after it fails, despite `$ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'`. Why?
hint: `git` is not a cmdlet.

choices.text: `git` writes its error to standard output
choices.why: Where it writes changes nothing about the preference.

choices.text: The preference applies inside functions alone
choices.why: It applies to the whole session.

choices.text: `git` exited with 0 despite the failure
choices.why: It exits non-zero; nothing is reading that.

choices.text: A native program has no ErrorAction to obey
choices.why: Correct. Check `$LASTEXITCODE` yourself, or `$?` on the very next line.

prompt: On this Linux machine, `Get-Service` reports that the term is not recognised. What does that mean?
hint: Look at the module list.

choices.text: The cmdlet is disabled and can be switched on
choices.why: There is no switch; it is not installed.

choices.text: Its module is not built for this platform
choices.why: Correct — that is why the lesson shows the error rather than inventing output.

choices.text: It needs elevated privileges before it will appear
choices.why: Privileges change what a command may do, not whether it exists.

choices.text: It was renamed in PowerShell 7
choices.why: `Get-Service` is still its name on Windows.

prompt: How does `Invoke-Command -ComputerName web01 { Get-Service }` differ from `ssh web01 'systemctl list-units'`?
hint: Think about what arrives back on your machine.

choices.text: It runs without a network connection
choices.why: Both need one.

choices.text: It encrypts the session, where ssh does not
choices.why: ssh encrypts everything by design.

choices.text: Objects come back, not text
choices.why: Correct — serialised on the far end and rehydrated here, so you can group and sort them.

choices.text: It targets a single machine at a time
choices.why: It takes a list, which is most of why people use it.

prompt: You are handed a Windows Server nobody documented. Which PowerShell should you assume is on it?
hint: One of the two ships in the box.

choices.text: The one that shipped with the box
choices.why: Yes — Windows PowerShell 5.1. PowerShell 7 is a separate install and a decision somebody has to make.

choices.text: PowerShell 7, since it is current
choices.why: It is current and it is not installed by default anywhere.

choices.text: Whichever the domain controller runs
choices.why: Versions are per machine, not per domain.

choices.text: Neither, until a role is installed
choices.why: 5.1 is there from the first boot.

prompt: Match each Windows-only cmdlet family to the Linux tool it stands in for.
hint: One of them has no single Linux equivalent at all.

prompt: Which bash tool has no PowerShell counterpart in the Rosetta table, and why?
hint: Three of the four rules explain the absence.

choices.text: `find`, because there is no recursive search
choices.why: `Get-ChildItem -Recurse` does exactly that.

choices.text: `sort`, because objects arrive pre-sorted
choices.why: `Sort-Object` exists and does the same job.

choices.text: `ssh`, because remoting works differently
choices.why: `Invoke-Command` is in the table, and it is the counterpart.

choices.text: `awk`, with no columns left to parse
choices.why: Correct — you take a property, so a field-extracting language has nothing to do.

prompt: Which of these are genuine advantages of the bash side?
hint: The lesson lists four, and two of these are not among them.

choices.text: it starts in three milliseconds
choices.why: Which is the whole argument for anything a scheduler runs on a timer.

choices.text: every program written in fifty years can join a pipeline
choices.why: Text is the lowest common denominator, and that is its strength.

choices.text: it is installed on every Linux machine already
choices.why: PowerShell is a download and a decision.

choices.text: filenames with spaces are handled more safely
choices.why: That is exactly what the object pipeline fixes and bash does not.

choices.text: arithmetic with decimals is built in
choices.why: `$(( ))` is integer only; lesson 9 sent you to `bc` for fractions.

prompt: Put this pipeline in the order that works.
trap: One of these destroys the objects, so it can only be last.

prompt: Three different bugs in this lesson all produce a plausible wrong answer with no error. Which is NOT one of them?
hint: Two are about types and one is about pipeline position.

choices.text: Comparing a CSV column against a number
choices.why: That one gave 16 rows where the truth is 7.

choices.text: Putting Format-Table in the middle of a pipeline
choices.why: That one gave a count of zero where eight rows matched.

choices.text: Calling Get-Service on a Linux machine
choices.why: Right — that one fails loudly, names the term, and stops. It is the honest kind.

choices.text: Sorting a CSV column without casting it
choices.why: That one put 8721 above 43731.

prompt: You need the three largest files in a directory. Which pipeline?
hint: Two stages, and their order matters.

choices.text: `Get-ChildItem | Sort-Object Length -Descending | Select-Object -First 3`
choices.why: Correct: sort everything, then take the top of it.

choices.text: `Get-ChildItem | Select-Object -First 3 | Sort-Object Length -Descending`
choices.why: That sorts three arbitrary files.

choices.text: `Get-ChildItem | Measure-Object Length -Maximum | Select-Object -First 3`
choices.why: That gives one statistic, not three files.

choices.text: `Get-ChildItem -Filter Length | Sort-Object -Descending`
choices.why: `-Filter` takes a name pattern, not a property.

prompt: A CSV column is text. Complete the cast that makes the comparison numeric: `Where-Object { ____$_.revenue -gt 30000 }`
hint: Five characters, including the brackets.

prompt: A colleague's script uses `ls`, `cat` and `sort` and works on their Windows laptop. What happens on a Linux server?
hint: Those three are aliases on one platform and real programs on the other.

choices.text: It fails immediately with unrecognised commands
choices.why: The commands exist on Linux — that is the problem.

choices.text: Different programs run, and the output changes
choices.why: Correct: on Linux those are the native tools, and they emit text rather than objects.

choices.text: It runs identically, because aliases are portable
choices.why: The aliases are created only where they do not collide.

choices.text: PowerShell rewrites them to the cmdlet names
choices.why: Nothing rewrites them; they resolve to whatever is found first.

prompt: Match each PowerShell cmdlet to the bash command it replaces.
hint: Two of them replace a pair of bash commands rather than one.

prompt: Which single habit would have prevented the most bugs in this lesson?
hint: Count how many sections mention the same thing.

choices.text: Writing `Get-ChildItem` instead of `gci`
choices.why: Good practice, and it prevents a different class of problem.

choices.text: Putting `-ErrorAction Stop` on each cmdlet
choices.why: Useful, and it does not touch the comparison or the sort.

choices.text: Running Get-Member on an unfamiliar object
choices.why: Excellent advice for learning, and it fixes nothing on its own.

choices.text: Casting text to a number at the boundary
choices.why: Correct — the filter, the sort and the arithmetic all went wrong on the same omission.

prompt: What is the PowerShell equivalent of `export X=1`?
hint: The environment is a drive, and there is a shorthand for it.

choices.text: `Set-Variable X 1 -Scope Global`
choices.why: That makes a shell variable, which a child process never sees.

choices.text: `$env:X = 1`
choices.why: Correct — the `env:` prefix is what makes it part of the environment.

choices.text: `New-Item Env:X -Value 1 -Force`
choices.why: It works and nobody writes it that way.

choices.text: `$global:X = 1`
choices.why: A global shell variable is still not in the environment.

prompt: `$((1+2))` in bash becomes what in PowerShell?
hint: Arithmetic needs no special syntax there.

choices.why: That is obsolete bash syntax, not PowerShell.
That is a subexpression containing a subexpression, and it is not how you add.
It works and nobody would write it for a sum.
Correct — every expression is evaluated, so arithmetic needs nothing around it.

prompt: A PowerShell function returns a number, but the caller gets two values. What is the likely cause?
hint: Something else in the body was not consumed.

choices.text: A stray expression nobody captured
choices.why: Correct — every uncaptured expression becomes output, so a bare `$x` on a line joins the result.

choices.text: `return` was used instead of `Write-Output`
choices.why: `return $x` emits `$x` and stops; it does not add anything extra.

choices.text: The function was called inside a pipeline
choices.why: The pipeline passes on what it is given; it does not add.

choices.text: The parameter was declared `[int]`
choices.why: A type on a parameter constrains the input, not the output.

prompt: Which of these is safe to run on a production machine without reading the documentation first?
hint: One verb group is defined as read-only.

choices.text: `Set-Service -Name X -StartupType Disabled`
choices.why: `Set-` overwrites, and this one stops a service coming back.

choices.text: `Remove-Item C:\Temp -Recurse`
choices.why: `Remove-` deletes, which is the point of the verb.

choices.text: `Get-CimInstance Win32_LogicalDisk`
choices.why: Right. `Get-` reads and returns; a `Get-` cmdlet that changed something would not have shipped.

choices.text: `New-Item HKCU:\Software\App`
choices.why: `New-` creates, which is a change even when it is a harmless one.

prompt: You are looking at an object and do not know what is on it. What do you type?
hint: One command answers that and nothing else does.

choices.text: `$obj | Format-List *`
choices.why: It shows the values it can render, and hides methods entirely.

choices.text: `$obj | Get-Member`
choices.why: Correct — the type name, every property and every method, in one table.

choices.text: `Get-Help $obj`
choices.why: Help documents commands, and an object is not one.

choices.text: `$obj.GetType()`
choices.why: That names the type and stops, leaving you to look it up.

prompt: Put these four questions in the order the one-question video asks them.
items: turn twelve hundred log lines into objects
group by status and sort by count
find the requests over three thousand milliseconds
group those by path to see which endpoint they are
trap: Nothing can be grouped until the text has become objects.

prompt: Both lessons 8 and 10 found the same twelve slow requests on the same endpoint. What did each pay for the answer?
hint: One paid at the start, the other paid all the way through.

choices.text: Bash paid zero; PowerShell paid one parse line for it
choices.why: Bash paid too — lesson 8 measured the cost, and it was not zero.

choices.text: Both paid about the same, so it comes down to taste
choices.why: The costs are real and different; taste is not the whole of it.

choices.text: PowerShell paid zero; bash paid in startup time alone
choices.why: Startup is real and is not what either lesson was measuring here.

choices.text: Bash counted columns; PowerShell built objects once
choices.why: Correct — and lesson 8 showed the column counting going wrong on a field with spaces in it.

prompt: Complete the cmdlet that tells you what an object has on it: `Get-ChildItem | ____`
hint: Two words with a hyphen.
